task.title: Planning the Build
task.shortdesc: Determine your budget and purpose before going shopping

context.p: The number of options in computer parts available is at the same time one of the prime reasons to build your own desktop and one of the prime obstacles to overcome. It is very easy to become overwhelmed with options without a plan, and just buying whatever looks good or is on sale is a sure route to compatibility issues and spending money on performance the rest of your machine cannot use. You need a plan before you start shopping for parts. Consider the following points before diving into parts list:

step.info: What are you going to do with your desktop that requires more power than a laptop or pre-built desktop? Do you need a powerful graphics card for 3D modelling and cutting-edge gaming graphics, or can you get by with a lesser option?

Costs for building a desktop can vary wildly, from a few hundred dollars to several thousand at the high end. Setting an overall target budget before you start will inform the general performance range to look at and roughly how much to spend on each component. There’s no point buying a high end $900 graphics card for a $1,000 total budget build, you won’t even be able to afford a power supply and case!

If you already have a desktop, some of the parts may be reusable, saving money out of your budget that can then be applied to other parts. Broadly speaking, all peripherals, such as a keyboard, mouse, monitor, or speakers, can be reused without problem assuming they still fit your needs. Legacy equipment, like a PS/2 mouse, might need replacement or at least an adapter for modern systems, but generally it’s not a problem. Some internal components can also be reused, but you will have to do research to see if they are compatible. In general, do not reuse power supplies, because they have limited lives and power supply faults can damage your new parts.

Computers are limited by their slowest part, something commonly called bottlenecking. A $900 graphics card is wasted on a build with a $50 processor and $50 worth of RAM because the rest of the machine will not be able to keep up with it. It is better to approximately match performance across parts so no one component is holding your desktop back.

I recommend planning your build around currently available parts that meet your current needs. In general, it’s not worth trying to anticipate future hardware trends and overspend on components now in order to stay ahead of the curve later. Cutting edge technology usually comes at a premium and will be outdated in six months. Pricing and availability are also influenced as much by geopolitics as advances in technology, meaning it can be difficult to guess how much a component will cost a year from now or what the state of the art will be.
